segments.titre: Jaclyn Bjorklund's lawsuit over semaglutide
segments.resume: Jaclyn Bjorklund's teeth began falling out in 2023 after more than a year on a weight-loss drug, which caused near-constant vomiting and several hospitalizations. She became one of the first people in the US to sue, and her case is now one of thousands. The drug is semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for diabetes and Wegovy for weight loss.
segments.texte: Jaclyn Bjorklund’s teeth started falling out sometime in 2023. It all stemmed from violent, near-constant vomiting. That started after more than a year on a drug her doctor prescribed for weight loss. She was hospitalized more than once, and that year, she became one of the first people in the country to sue over it. Today, her case is one of thousands. The drug was semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for diabetes, Wegovy for weight loss.

segments.titre: What is inside the shot: the video's roadmap
segments.resume: The narrator says everyone knows the basic deal of the drug but few ask what the money is buying. The video promises to explain how semaglutide rewrites a gut-to-brain signal, why it took the study of lizard venom to discover, and why the fine print is longer than the hype suggested.
segments.texte: By now, everybody already knows the basic deal. If you've got money to burn, you don't have to be fat anymore. What most people never ask is what their money is really buying. What is inside the shot. So today, we're breaking down how this drug rewrites a signal between your gut and your brain, why it took the study of lizard venom to figure out, and why the fine print turns out to be a lot longer than the hype ever let on.

segments.titre: Dr. Oz segment in 2021: a diabetes drug with an odd side effect
segments.resume: Drug origin stories are usually boring, and this one starts with a 2021 Dr. Oz TV segment on a new diabetes injection whose patients kept losing weight unintentionally. Semaglutide was then a decade-old idea prescribed to a few million diabetics and culturally irrelevant.
segments.texte: Every drug has an origin story. Most of them are boring. This one starts with a segment on daytime TV that almost nobody remembers watching because most did not. In February 2021, the Dr. Oz show ran a piece on a new diabetes injection with an odd side effect. Patients kept losing weight they weren’t trying to lose. At the time, it barely registered. Semaglutide was a decade-old idea wearing a new brand name, prescribed by endocrinologists to a few million diabetics, and about as culturally relevant as a rounding error.

segments.titre: Elon Musk's tweet and the explosion in prescriptions
segments.resume: On October 1, 2022, Elon Musk tweeted that fasting and Wegovy had made him lean. Prescriptions rose 442 percent within about a year, and by the end of 2023 1.7% of Americans had been prescribed a semaglutide drug, a 40x increase in five years. Ozempic became a punchline, a flex, a celebrity rumor and a diagnosis.
segments.texte: Then, on October 1, 2022, Elon Musk answered a fan’s question on Twitter about how he’d gotten lean. His answer was fasting and a drug called Wegovy. One tweet, from one of the most-followed accounts (and soon-to-be-owner) of the platform, did more for this drug's fame than a decade of clinical trials ever managed. Within about a year, semaglutide prescriptions had climbed 442 percent, and the word Ozempic stopped being a drug. By the end of 2023, 1.7% of all Americans had been prescribed a semaglutide medication that year alone, a 40x increase over the past five years. Soon, Ozempic and Wegovy became a punchline, a flex, a rumor about your favorite celebrity, and a diagnosis all rolled into one, depending on who was saying the name and how they meant it.

segments.titre: Novo Nordisk becomes Europe's most valuable company
segments.resume: In September 2023 Novo Nordisk overtook LVMH to become the most valuable public company in Europe, worth more than the Danish economy. Its drugs helped some 39 million people in six months and obesity-drug sales grew 154%. The narrator stresses this was no fad: semaglutide was the first drug shown in controlled trials that appetite runs on a hormonal signal.
segments.texte: The money behind that name grew just as fast. In September 2023, Novo Nordisk, the Danish company that makes both Ozempic and Wegovy, overtook LVMH to become the most valuable public company in Europe, worth more than the entire Danish economy. By the end of that year, the company said its drugs had helped some 39 million people worldwide in six months alone, while obesity-drug sales grew 154% year over year. Suddenly a pharmaceutical company built on a diabetes injection was outperforming the luxury goods conglomerate that owns Louis Vuitton. This wasn’t a fad, and it wasn’t a trick. Semaglutide was the first drug in history to prove in controlled clinical trials that appetite itself runs on a hormonal signal, and that if you can control that signal, you can control your hunger.

segments.titre: Shortages, compounding pharmacies and counterfeit Ozempic
segments.resume: Wegovy joined the FDA drug shortage list in March 2022 and Ozempic followed, leaving diabetics struggling to get their medication. Compounding pharmacies, some legal under the shortage exemption and some not, moved in, followed by counterfeiters. In one documented case patients received mislabeled insulin and were hospitalized with seizures and dangerously low blood sugar.
segments.texte: Demand did what it always does when a drug this good meets a culture this hungry for a shortcut. By March 2022, Wegovy was formally added to the FDA’s drug shortage list. Ozempic soon followed. For the actual diabetics this drug was built for, the shortage meant medication they depended on to manage their blood sugar was suddenly difficult to reliably obtain. Millions of people without diabetes were now competing for the same pens. Into that gap walked compounding pharmacies, some operating legally under the FDA’s own shortage exemption, some not. And then came the counterfeiters. Fake Ozempic started to turn up in pharmacies across the United States and Europe, and in at least one documented case, patients did not even get a weak knockoff. They got actual insulin, mislabeled as semaglutide, and ended up hospitalized with seizures and dangerously low blood sugar as a result. Ultimately, a drug that promised to fix a broken signal in the body ended up exposing a much older one: Where there’s enough money and convenience on the table, the guardrails come off fast.

segments.titre: How GLP-1 works: pancreas, vagus nerve and hypothalamus
segments.resume: GLP-1 is a gut hormone released in a burst when you eat, doing three things: it prompts the pancreas to release insulin only when blood sugar is high, acts on vagus nerve receptors to slow stomach emptying, and reaches the hypothalamus. There it quiets the NPY-AgRP hunger neurons and switches on neurons that signal fullness.
segments.texte: But how does it actually work? Semaglutide drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy hinge on a hormone almost nobody outside a biochemistry lab has ever heard of: GLP-1, or glugagon-like-peptide-1. Every time you eat, your guy releases a small burst of it. GLP-1 does three things simultaneously when that happens. It tells your pancreas to release insulin, but only when your blood sugar is actually elevated, which is actually a built-in safety feature that keeps it from crashing your glucose the way some diabetes drugs can. It also hits receptors on your vagus nerve, the long cable running between your gut and your brainstem which slows down how fast your stomach empties into the small intestine. And finally, it makes a little trip to your hypothalamus, the walnut-sized command center that regulates hunger. Once there, it quiets a set of neurons called NPY-AgRP responsible for that gnawing feeling of needing to take a bite of everything and anything nearby, conveniently switching on a different set of receptor neurons which signal fullness. In other words, GLP-1 is responsible for flipping a switch between two competing populations of brain cells that have been arguing over your next meal since before you were born.

segments.titre: Engineering semaglutide to last a week
segments.resume: Natural GLP-1 is destroyed by the enzyme DPP-4 in about two minutes. Semaglutide is about 94% identical to human GLP-1 but has two amino acids swapped so DPP-4 cannot grip it, plus a fatty side chain that binds albumin and shields it from enzymes. The signal therefore lasts about a week per injection.
segments.texte: The catch is that GLP-1 in its natural state barely survives inside you for very long. An enzyme called DPP-4 is also present, which tears it apart in about two minutes flat. Sometimes you can blink, and the GLP-1 signal is gone. Semaglutide is what happens when chemists rebuild the same molecule from scratch, then armor-plate it for battle in your bloodstream. It’s about 94% identical to your own GLP-1, but with two amino acids swapped out so DPP-4 can’t get a grip on it. It’s also got this fatty side-chain attached to one of its amino acids that lets it clamp onto albumin, the most abundant protein in your bloodstream. Once it’s riding around bound to albumin, it’s essentially invisible to the enzymes that would normally destroy it. That’s how you get a signal that used to last two minutes suddenly lasting about a week. With just one injection, your hypothalamus can spend the next seven days being told, on a loop, that the fuel crisis is over. No more late night crash outs at the fast food drive through window.

segments.titre: Delayed gastric emptying and why nausea is common
segments.resume: Scintigraphy studies using radioactive tracers found that 37% of people on long-acting semaglutide still had food in their stomachs four hours after eating, versus none on placebo. Food is both less appealing and physically retained longer, which prolongs fullness and explains why nausea is the most common complaint of new users.
segments.texte: That’s the science of everything on the appetite side. But the stomach side is just as real. Scintigraphy studies, which is what they call the radioactive tracer that lets researchers watch food moving through someone’s gut in real time, have found that 37% of people on long-acting semaglutide still had measurable food sitting in their stomachs four hours after eating while the placebo group had none. With semaglutide, food is both less appealing and physically packed longer, which is a big part of why fullness lasts so long after a meal. That is also, not coincidentally, why nausea is the most common complaint among new users. It might feel like you’re imagining that queasy, overfull feeling, but your stomach is genuinely moving slower than it’s built to.

segments.titre: The slow dose ramp-up and the nausea trade-off
segments.resume: Prescriptions start at about 0.25 mg a week and climb over four to five months to a 2.4 mg maintenance dose, giving GLP-1 receptors and the gut time to adjust. A pilot study comparing an eight-week and a sixteen-week ramp found 20% quit from nausea in the fast group versus about 2% in the slow group, with identical final results.
segments.texte: So many people’s first weeks on this drug feel miserable for a reason. The dosing schedule is akin to damage control. Every semaglutide prescription starts absurdly low, around 0.25 milligrams a week, which is a fraction of the dose that actually produces meaningful weight loss. This climbs slowly over the next four to five months from 0.25 to 0.5 to 1 to 1.7 to a maintenance dose of 2.4 milligrams. The crawl is a calculated necessity, since the body’s GLP-1 receptors and the gut’s tolerance for delayed gastric emptying need time to adjust to a signal running at that intensity. If you were to jump straight to the therapeutic dose, the nausea and vomiting would become severe enough that most people would simply quit. The data on this is stark. When a diabetes population pilot study tested semaglutide dosing levels head-to-head in an eight week ramp up versus sixteen weeks, they found the rush group quit because of nausea 20% of the time. In the slower group, barely 2% bailed. Both groups ended up at the same dose, with the same results, one just calmer about getting there. So the nausea you get on semaglutide is basically your body’s way of giving you a speeding ticket. Slam your foot on the gas and tell your body it will never starve again faster than it’s built to process, and it fights back the only way it knows how. Ease off, give it a few months to adjust rather than a few weeks, and most people barely feel the climb at all.

segments.titre: Three mechanisms together: brain, stomach and reward
segments.resume: Combining the three mechanisms, the brain stops signaling hunger, the stomach empties more slowly and the reward system stops caring, which rewrites the biological conversation that let someone become obese. The narrator calls it an elegant solution but says semaglutide's origins are less elegant.
segments.texte: When you put all three mechanisms together–the brain stopping to signal hunger, the stomach that stops emptying itself quickly, and a reward system that stops caring, you get a drug that can quietly rewrite the actual biological conversations that enabled someone to become obese in the first place. An elegant solution to be sure, but semaglutide’s origins are less so.

segments.titre: The Gila monster and its blood sugar mystery
segments.resume: The Gila monster of the Sonoran desert eats only a few times a year, spending over 90% of its life motionless underground. Despite living off one huge meal for months it never crashes its blood sugar. For decades this was seen as a mere curiosity, a fun fact good for parties or Jeopardy.
segments.texte: Somewhere in the Sonoran desert, there’s a lizard that eats five or six times a year and considers that a perfectly reasonable schedule. That’s because the Gila monster spends over 90% of its life doing absolutely nothing buried underground. Laying motionless, it lives off one enormous meal for months at a stretch, or about 4-5 per year. And somehow throughout this process, it never crashes its blood sugar in the way a human would after skipping lunch twice in a row. For decades nobody thought the fact was useful for anything except impressing people at parties or possibly winning a round of Jeopardy under the category, “Ozempic Origins.”

segments.titre: Dr. John Eng and the venom fishing expedition
segments.resume: In the early 1990s endocrinologist John Eng, who worked at the Bronx VA Medical Center and trained under Nobel laureate Rosalyn Yalow, used her hormone-detection technique on Gila monster saliva. His collaborator Jean-Pierre Raufman drove test tubes from Brooklyn to the Bronx in a Toyota Camry. Nobody expected a blockbuster; it was a fishing expedition.
segments.texte: Then, in the early 1990s, an endocrinologist named Dr. John Eng got curious about the why. Eng worked at the Bronx VA Medical Center, and he’d trained under Rosalyn Yalow, a Nobel laureate who’d invented a technique for detecting microscopic traces of hormones in blood. Eng turned that same tool on Gila monster saliva in the hopes of figuring out if whatever let this lizard skip meals for months without consequence might be doing something worth understanding. His collaborator, Dr. Jean-Pierre Raufman, handled the unglamorous part–driving test tubes from Brooklyn to the Bronx in his Toyota Camry, sometimes several times a week, for a project he'd later describe as basically a fishing expedition. Nobody involved thought they were building a blockbuster. They were just chasing a strange animal fact wherever it led.

segments.titre: Exendin-4: the lizard's slow-release GLP-1
segments.resume: In 1992 Eng isolated exendin-4, a 39-amino-acid peptide from the venom, about 53% identical to human GLP-1. Human GLP-1 breaks down in roughly a minute while exendin-4 kept working for hours, making the lizard's hormone a naturally slow-release version of the hormone behind today's pharmacy shelves.
segments.texte: And in 1992, it actually led somewhere. Eng isolated a new peptide from the venom, a 39-amino-acid molecule he named exendin-4. Structurally, it was about 53 percent identical to a human hormone called GLP-1 but with one critical difference. Human GLP-1 breaks down in the bloodstream in roughly a minute. Exendin-4 kept working for hours. The lizard, it turned out, was walking around with a naturally slow-release version of the exact hormone that would eventually fill an entire aisle of your pharmacy.

segments.titre: Rejection, Amylin and the Eli Lilly partnership
segments.resume: The VA showed no interest in patenting the discovery, since lizard venom was not combat related, and pharmaceutical companies passed because peptide drugs were seen as fragile and expensive. A small San Diego biotech, Amylin Pharmaceuticals, took the idea on and by 2002 had about a year of cash left until Eli Lilly's $350 million partnership kept it alive.
segments.texte: The story probably should have ended there. But Eng brought the discovery to the VA expecting some interest in patenting it. No doing. Since lizard venom wasn’t technically combat related, it wasn’t their commercial concern. He spent the next few years pitching pharmaceutical companies who mostly scratched their heads and passed. Peptide drugs had a reputation in the 1990s for being fragile and expensive to manufacture, which was ironically the exact same problem exendin-4's slow decay rate happened to solve. Nobody made that connection for years. Eventually, a small San Diego biotech company took a punt on Eng’s idea. It nearly sank the company. Burning through its funding for years with nothing to put onto the market, by 2002 Amylin Pharmaceuticals had roughly one year of cash left before Eli Lilly stepped in with a $350 million partnership that kept the lights on. That deal is the reason any of this ever reached a pharmacy shelf.

segments.titre: From Byetta in 2005 to Ozempic: a quarter-century overnight success
segments.resume: The FDA approved Byetta in 2005 as the first GLP-1 drug, but it needed two injections a day, caused nausea in nearly half of trial patients and was not a hit. Novo Nordisk then reached once-daily dosing with Victoza in 2010 and once-weekly in 2017 with semaglutide, using a fatty anchor to bind a blood protein, branded Ozempic and Wegovy.
segments.texte: In 2005, the FDA approved the result, known as Byetta, the first GLP-1 drug in history. It required two injections per day, every day, and nearly half of trial patients dealt with nausea. Byetta wasn’t a big hit, and it showed in how few patients actually stuck with it long-term. The real bottleneck was the clock. Every improvement after Byetta was a fight against that same two-minute decay rate GLP-1 has always had. Novo Nordisk got it to once a day in 2010, with a drug called Victoza. In 2017, they cracked once a week entirely, using a fatty molecular anchor that let the hormone hitch a ride on a blood protein instead of getting torn apart on its own. That drug is the one you've actually heard of. They called it semaglutide. They branded it Ozempic and Wegovy. And so it took the better part of twenty-five years to get from lizard peptides to “everyone knows at least one person on this drug.” Overnight success, as usual, took a quarter century to build.

segments.titre: Why weight loss alone is not enough for a drug
segments.resume: The narrator asks whether GLP-1 drugs could be taken seriously by cardiologists and doctors. Weight loss alone is a weak marker in clinical trials since many interventions shrink waistlines without changing outcomes like survival, so semaglutide had to clear a higher bar than moving the scale.
segments.texte: But after all of the effort it took to make GLP-1 a reality, was it even in a place where cardiologists and medical doctors could take it seriously? Let’s put that another way. Weight loss alone has never been that impressive of a marker as a drug passes through its clinical trials. Plenty of interventions can shrink a waistline without changing a single outcome that actually matters, like whether a person will survive into the next decade. In other words, Semaglutide had to clear a much higher bar than whether it moved the scale for its users or not. And as it turns out, it does. Here’s what the data actually shows.

segments.titre: STEP trials: about 15 percent weight loss
segments.resume: In the STEP trials that led to Wegovy's approval, participants lost around 15% of body weight over roughly a year and a half, over 30 pounds for a 220-pound person, without gym visits or calorie tracking. Earlier diet interventions topped out around 3 to 5% and usually regained weight, so semaglutide looked like a different category.
segments.texte: In the STEP trials that actually got semaglutide approved for weight loss under the brand name Wegovy, participants lost an average of about 15 percent of their total body weight over roughly a year and a half. For a 220 pound person, that’s over 30 pounds shed from a once weekly injection, all without a single trip to the gym or calorie tracked. Compare that to the track record of basically every other diet intervention before this, which all topped off at around 3 to 5%, and even that modest number would almost always creep back after a couple of years. In that context, semaglutide started to look like a different category of result entirely.

segments.titre: SELECT trial: 20% cut in cardiovascular risk
segments.resume: The SELECT trial followed over 17,600 overweight or obese non-diabetic people with existing cardiovascular disease, and semaglutide cut their composite risk of heart attack or stroke by 20%. Weight loss was lower than in STEP because the trial tested heart protection independent of weight, making it the first weight-loss-adjacent drug to reduce cardiac events.
segments.texte: What actually got cardiologists paying attention was a separate trial called SELECT, which followed over 17,600 people who already had cardiovascular disease and were overweight or obese, but not diabetic. These were people with real, measurable risk of a heart attack or stroke. In that group, semaglutide cut their composite risk by 20%. In that specific trial, it’s worth mentioning that the weight loss averaged lower than the STEP trial’s 15%, but that’s because SELECT wasn’t optimized for weight loss but rather testing whether the drug protected the heart independent of how much weight came off. And the answer was yes. This was the first time a weight-loss adjacent drug had ever proven that it could reduce actual cardiac events.

segments.titre: Food noise and GLP-1 receptors in the reward circuitry
segments.resume: Patients reported an unanticipated effect: their food noise, the constant mental static urging them to eat, went quiet. This fits the brain biology, since GLP-1 receptors sit in reward circuitry also involved in cravings for nicotine and alcohol, not just food.
segments.texte: The side-effect nobody anticipated but patients started reporting before researchers had even coined a term for it was that their “food noise” had gone down. The constant low-grade mental static telling you to eat something, wondering what’s in the fridge, doing all this despite you having finished your last meal within the last hour suddenly started to stop being generated in the first place. This tracks with what’s actually happening in the brain; GLP-1 receptors sit in the same reward circuitry, which is the same real estate involved in cravings for nicotine and alcohol, not just food.

segments.titre: Alcohol and smoking: semaglutide against addiction
segments.resume: A placebo-controlled trial in alcohol use disorder found semaglutide reduced weekly cravings, drinks per drinking day and heavy drinking days, and research on smokers showed larger reductions in cigarettes per day. The drug was never designed for addiction, but the hunger signal influences many more impulses than expected.
segments.texte: That’s led to one of the stranger side stories in the whole saga. A placebo-controlled trial testing semaglutide specifically for alcohol use disorder found it actually reduced weekly cravings, average drinks per drinking day, and heavy drinking days, compared to placebo. Separate research on smokers found people on semaglutide cut their cigarettes per day significantly more than people who weren't. Nobody built this drug to treat addiction. It was designed to talk to a hunger signal, and it turned out that same signal has its fingers in a lot more of your impulses than anyone expected.

segments.titre: FLOW trial: kidney disease and a trial stopped early
segments.resume: The FLOW trial of people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease found semaglutide cut major kidney events, cardiovascular events and death by 24%. It was stopped early because the benefits were so obvious that continuing to give half the participants a placebo looked unethical.
segments.texte: It didn’t stop at hearts and cravings either. A separate trial called FLOW followed people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease–the same population staring down dialysis in the face–and found semaglutide cut the risk of major kidney events, cardiovascular events, and death by 24%. That trial got stopped early, but not because anything went wrong. The research team simply felt the benefits were so obvious that continuing to give half the participants a placebo started to look unethical.

segments.titre: Knee osteoarthritis pain relief
segments.resume: In a trial of 407 people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis, the semaglutide group reported significantly more pain relief. Less body weight means less joint load, but researchers also suspect an effect on body-wide inflammation beyond the mechanical benefit.
segments.texte: And what about knee-pain, of all things? In a trial of 407 people with both obesity and knee osteoarthritis, the semaglutide group reported significantly more relief on a standard osteoarthritis pain scale. Some of that is simple physics; less physical weight means less load on a joint that’s been grinding under it for years. But researchers also suspect part of it comes from semaglutide’s effect on inflammation throughout the body more so than the mechanical math of pounds on cartilage.

segments.titre: One hormone, five organ systems
segments.resume: The narrator notes a pattern: a once-weekly diabetes shot has ended up touching the heart, kidneys, joints and the reward pathways behind addiction. Five different organ systems are affected by one hormone few people had heard of a decade earlier.
segments.texte: By this point, a pattern should start to appear. This all started as a once-weekly diabetes shot. It’s ended up touching the heart, the kidneys, the joints, and the reward pathways that drive addiction. Five completely different organ systems affected by one hormone few people had heard of a decade ago.

segments.titre: Gambling claims: ahead of the data
segments.resume: Claims that semaglutide can cure gambling are theoretical extrapolations from the shared reward-pathway biology and are not backed by clinical trials the way smoking and alcohol are. Anyone saying it cures gambling is a few years ahead of the data.
segments.texte: Now, before this turns into an infomercial you should know that gambling gets mentioned a lot in this curing of vices conversation too. That’s worth being honest about up front. It’s all mostly theoretical, extrapolated conclusions from the same shared reward-pathway biology from earlier. None of that is backed by clinical trials the way smoking and alcohol are. So if someone you know tells you that semaglutide can cure gambling, they’re a few years ahead of the data.

segments.titre: Nothing this good comes without risks: reading the fine print
segments.resume: Putting the benefits together, semaglutide does far more than anyone expected, which should make people suspicious. Every win comes with an asterisk, and the narrator moves on to the fine print and the risks.
segments.texte: Regardless, put it all together and you’ve got a drug that does far more than anyone would have originally bet. Which is exactly the kind of result that should also make you suspicious. Nothing this good comes without risks. And semaglutide doesn’t, either. Every one of the aforementioned wins comes with an asterisk attached; now it’s time to actually read the fine print.

segments.titre: Muscle loss: about 40 percent of weight lost is lean mass
segments.resume: Research presented at the Endocrine Society's 2025 meeting found roughly 40% of weight lost on semaglutide is lean mass. Older adults, women and people eating less protein are at highest risk, while people who ate more protein held onto significantly more muscle, so outcomes depend on diet and exercise.
segments.texte: Start with muscle. When your body is told repeatedly that a famine has arrived and it’s time to burn the reserves, it doesn't neatly sort fat from muscle on the way out. Research presented at the Endocrine Society’s 2025 meeting found that roughly 40% of the weight people lose on semaglutide is lean mass. Muscle, in other words, not fat. And they added that older adults, women, and people eating less protein were at the highest risk of losing more of it. 40% isn’t a fixed cost, either. The same research found that people who ate more protein while on the drug held onto significantly more muscle. In other words, semaglutide will happily burn through your muscle right alongside the fat reserves if you let it. Whether it actually does comes down to what you’re doing at the dinner table and the gym, not the drug itself.

segments.titre: What causes Ozempic face
segments.resume: Ozempic face comes from losing facial fat and muscle along with the rest of the body, so skin loses the volume beneath it. This is what rapid weight loss has always done to faces, and semaglutide made rapid weight loss common enough to need a name.
segments.texte: This is also, in large part, where “Ozempic face” comes from. Lose fat and muscle from your face at the same time you’re losing it everywhere else, and skin that used to have volume underneath it just doesn’t anymore. That’s what rapid weight loss has always done to a face, and semaglutide just made rapid weight loss common enough that people started needing a name for it.

segments.titre: Stopping semaglutide: discontinuation and weight regain
segments.resume: Two-thirds of people had stopped GLP-1 drugs within a year, and most who stop regain roughly half to two-thirds of the weight, even with healthy habits. Real-world health-record data are somewhat less grim, but for most people the injections are like paying rent: stop and the hunger returns.
segments.texte: So what happens when you stop the injections? The same as what tends to happen when you stop dieting or exercising. Clinical follow-up data on people who discontinued semaglutide found that two-thirds of people had stopped taking GLP-1 drugs within a year. Even with healthy habits, most people who stop are shown to regain roughly half to two-thirds of their weight back. Real world data pulled from electronic health records paint a slightly less grim picture, with a meaningful share of people holding steady or continuing to lose even after stopping. But the core trial finding stands: for most people, the injections are just like paying rent. Stop paying it, and the hunger you outsourced to a weekly injection comes back to collect.

segments.titre: Gastroparesis, GLP-1 usage and the lawsuits
segments.resume: Slowing gastric emptying can go too far and cause gastroparesis, a stomach that essentially stops emptying. KFF reports over 31 million Americans, about 12% of adults, use a GLP-1 drug, and at least 4,400 have sued over inadequate warnings, with 75% alleging gastroparesis and others citing blockages, gallbladder injuries, gangrenous tissue, reflux and abdominal pain.
segments.texte: On the gastrointestinal side, the drug’s reputation starts to get genuinely ugly. Slowing gastric emptying is the whole point of the mechanism, but push that too far in the wrong place and you get gastroparesis, a stomach that essentially stops emptying at all. More than 31 million Americans, or about 12% of all adults, are currently on a GLP-1 drug, according to health policy nonprofit KFF. Out of that enormous population, a fraction of at least 4,400 people have now filed lawsuits alleging the drugmakers did not adequately warn them what they were signing up for. 75% of these allege gastroparesis, with others claiming intestinal blockages, gallbladder injuries, gangrenous tissue, chronic acid reflux, abdominal pain and related complications.

segments.titre: NAION vision loss and the case of Todd Engel
segments.resume: In June 2025 European regulators added NAION, a sudden and often permanent vision loss, to the Ozempic label, warning it may affect up to 1 in 10,000 patients. Maryland truck driver Todd Engel lost sight in one eye four months into Ozempic and the other ten months later, becoming legally blind and losing his license and job. US labels do not name NAION.
segments.texte: Another newer finding that hasn’t made it into most of the celebrity coverage yet either is that in June 2025, European regulators added a rare but serious vision condition called NAION to the official Ozempic label. NAION is a sudden, often permanent vision loss. It’s rare. But Todd Engel found out the hard way that a vague warning on a drug label could mean something much worse. Four months into taking Ozempic for his diabetes, the Maryland truck driver woke up one December morning and couldn’t see out of one eye. Doctors diagnosed him with NAION, sometimes called an eye stroke which stems from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve. Ten months later, he woke up again, turned to his wife, and told her the other eye had gone dark too. Engel is now legally blind. He’d lost his commercial license, his job, and the ability to watch his grandkids play baseball.
